title: Telephone switchboard: optical circuit switch re-patches memory sleds
idea: An operator plugging cords: a MEMS optical circuit switch at rack level connects any socket's CXL links to any memory sled, re-patched every few minutes by a scheduler, so stranded memory on one server becomes another's without packet-switch latency or buffering.
why: About 25% of datacenter DRAM is stranded; circuit-switched pooling recovers most of it at near direct-attach latency.

title: Sourdough starter: pages kept as regenerable seed-plus-recipe stubs
idea: Forced connection: a baker keeps a pinch of starter, not the bread. Add an MMU/OS page class 'regenerable' whose PTE points to a 64-byte recipe (PRNG seed, generator kernel ID, parameters); on fault a near-memory engine re-materialises the 4 KB page in ~1 us and under pressure the page is simply dropped instead of swapped. Targets init weights, RoPE/sin tables, lookup tables, decompressed assets, pattern pages and deterministic intermediates.
why: Cost per bit / capacity: 5-25% of resident footprint in AI and HPC jobs is derivable; dropping instead of storing it gives 1.05-1.3x effective capacity with no new DRAM.

title: Predictive line coding: memory stores only what it could not guess
idea: Po: memory that lies, then gets corrected. A tiny predictor in the memory controller guesses each 64 B line from address neighbors and a per-page learned context (strides, pointer bases, float exponents); DRAM stores only the residual, which is near-zero for most lines and packed into variable-size slots, like inter-frame video coding for RAM.
why: 2-4x effective capacity on heaps and tensors where generic LZ gets ~1.5x; attacks cost per bit with no new cell.

title: Shared inverted page tables end per-process mapping copies
idea: Reverse the page-table direction for shared memory: one table per shared physical region (indexed by frame, or a kernel-shared upper-level table) is linked into every process that maps it, instead of each of hundreds of database worker processes building its own copy.
why: Databases with large shared buffers can burn tens of GB on duplicate page tables; sharing them recovers that DRAM with a kernel change alone.

title: Bit-significance-partitioned refresh for approximate tensors
idea: This adds zero masks. The allocator lays out tensors so that sign, exponent and high-mantissa bits sit in different rows from low-mantissa bits. The controller refreshes high-significance rows normally and low-significance rows 8-16x less often, using per-row directed refresh. Refresh time is matched to the importance of each bit.
why: It recovers 50-80% of refresh energy and bandwidth on tensor regions (fact 3), with errors confined to LSBs: approximate memory with no new cells.

title: Confidential-computing integrity MACs reused as dedup fingerprints
idea: Combine the per-line MACs and integrity tree that memory-encryption engines (TDX/SEV-SNP style) already compute with a deduplication index: read-only pages encrypted under a shared convergent 'dedup key domain' produce identical MAC roots, so the controller detects and merges them without decrypting.
why: Encrypted VMs currently make page dedup impossible; this regains 15-30% of host memory in confidential clouds with zero extra hashing hardware.

title: Forward-only training: learn without storing the forward pass
idea: Po: training forgets the forward pass. Gradients come from forward-mode derivatives (JVPs with random tangents, variance-reduced by local layer-wise losses), so no activations are kept for backprop and memory stays O(one layer) regardless of depth.
why: Activations are often >50% of training memory; removing them could cut training DRAM/HBM 2-5x if the convergence penalty is contained.

title: Pea-pod DIMMs with socketed packages replaced one at a time
idea: Like peas pulled from a pod, DRAM packages sit in low-profile LGA micro-sockets on the module, so one failing package is swapped in minutes and firmware remaps its range, instead of scrapping a 64-128 GB DIMM for one bad chip.
why: Repair: cuts DIMM scrap by ~80%, shrinking replacement DRAM demand.

title: Optane latency, fixed: look-ahead MoE router hides flash fetch
idea: Optane failed partly because software could not hide its latency on unpredictable accesses. Co-design the model instead: train each MoE router to choose experts for layer L+2 from layer L's hidden state, giving two layers of warning to fetch expert weights from flash into SRAM before they are needed.
why: MoE models with hundreds of GB of experts serve from flash plus SRAM, driving weight DRAM toward zero.

title: Swap fixed-precision KV for age-graded fading precision
idea: Substitute uniform precision with human-like memory decay. KV entries are written at 8 bits; a background kernel requantizes them to 4 bits after ~1k tokens and 2 bits after ~8k, then evicts them, unless their cumulative attention mass marks them salient. This is pure software on unchanged HBM.
why: Long contexts average about 3 bits per element instead of 16, a ~5x KV cut that keeps important tokens sharp.

title: Lisp-machine cdr-coding revived as hardware next-pointer elision
idea: Symbolics/LMI cdr-coding replaced next-pointers with 2-bit tags when list cells were contiguous, and died with Lisp machines. Add a memory-side 'implicit successor' bit per 16 B chunk: allocators place linked nodes contiguously, the controller drops the 8 B pointer whenever next == this+size, and reconstructs it on load.
why: Linked lists, trees and graph adjacency structures lose 25-50% of their bytes, shrinking DRAM for pointer-chasing workloads.

title: One shared latent per token across all layers, VQ-coded
idea: Worsen: store separate K and V for every head of every layer at fp16. Flip: train models to emit one small latent per token that all layers up-project from (cross-layer multi-head latent attention), then vector-quantize that latent to a 1-2 byte codebook index.
why: Cost and capacity: 100-300x smaller KV per token; trades retraining and some quality.

title: Eliminate the guest OS inside every VM with unikernel images
idea: Compile cloud services as unikernels or library OSes that link only the kernel functions they use, removing the 200 MB-1 GB guest kernel, init system and page cache that each VM duplicates.
why: Dense VM hosts carrying hundreds of guests recover 10-30% of host DRAM.

title: Magnesium-light pointers: hardware-compressed 64-bit pointers in memory
idea: Magnesium cuts vehicle weight without losing strength; a load/store extension keeps 64-bit pointers in memory as 32-bit offsets from one of 16 region-base registers selected by 4 tag bits, expanding on load and compressing on store, which generalizes JVM compressed oops to C/C++/Rust heaps transparently.
why: Pointer-heavy data (graphs, trees, JS/Python objects) is 30-60% pointers; halving them saves ~15-30% DRAM for those workloads (density).

title: Recommender long tail: synthesize rare-ID embeddings from features
idea: From the largest single DRAM user, ad recommenders with TB-scale embedding tables: only IDs seen more than N times get a stored row, and every tail ID's embedding is computed on the fly by a small feature tower from side attributes (category, text, graph neighbors) trained jointly with the model.
why: 90%+ of embedding rows are long-tail IDs touched rarely; synthesizing them cuts embedding DRAM 5-10x.

title: Peltier-cooled DRAM island inside a 125 C module
idea: Mount one small LPDDR die on a thin-film Bi2Te3 Peltier cooler held at 85 C, and keep the rest of the working set in heat-tolerant NVM (AlScN FeFET or Ge-rich PCM). The cooled island holds only the hottest 10-15% of data, so cooling costs just a few watts.
why: Most data avoids 4x refresh and retention failure at 125 C, and DRAM per ECU drops 5-10x.

title: Magnify the time axis: diurnal DRAM time-sharing
idea: Magnify memory scheduling from space to time: serving fleets lend 30-50% of their DRAM through CXL pooling to batch, ETL and training-data jobs off-peak. Pages come back within seconds via compressed swap when traffic rises.
why: Provisioning for peak strands DRAM. Time-sharing cuts total provisioned DRAM ~20-35%.

title: Spin-Hall stochastic writes keep an attention-weighted KV reservoir
idea: When a token's KV arrives, a spin-Hall (beta-W) current pulse tries to switch a low-barrier MTJ, with amplitude set by the token's running attention score. The switching probability equals the keep probability, so the KV buffer becomes a hardware importance-weighted reservoir sample of the context. Only switched tokens are written to the fixed-size KV store; dropped ones are compensated by unbiased reweighting.
why: Caps KV memory at a fixed budget (4-10x smaller) while keeping attention estimates unbiased. One device per token replaces digital PRNG and sort logic.

title: Iridium's rainbow: spectral KV keeps only low-frequency sequence components
idea: Iridium is named for the rainbow; along the sequence axis, each head's K and V for closed 256-token blocks are DCT-transformed and only the 32-64 highest-energy coefficients are kept, with attention over old blocks run on the inverse transform or directly in the frequency domain.
why: Hidden states drift slowly across neighboring tokens, so KV for distant context compresses 4-8x with bounded error (density, cost/bit).

title: Value prediction, fixed: store only predictor residuals off critical path
idea: Load-value prediction never entered CPUs because mispredictions cost pipeline flushes. Reuse stride, context and small learned predictors as a memory codec: on write store only the residual from the prediction in SRAM or flash, on read run the predictor and add the residual, so a misprediction costs only extra bits.
why: Smooth data (sensor streams, counters, indices, embeddings) compresses 2-5x, letting SRAM/flash-only devices hold working sets that used to need DRAM.

title: Librarian's closed stacks: garbage collector exiles cold objects to NVMe
idea: Libraries keep rarely requested books in closed stacks. A modified generational GC (OpenJDK or Go) samples object reads with 1% read barriers. Objects untouched for N collections are compacted into closed-stack regions and madvised out to NVMe, with forwarding pointers so a touch faults back the whole batch. Fundable as a 24-month, 3-person project.
why: Managed heaps are sized 2-3x their live data and hold large cold populations. Object-granular exile cuts heap DRAM 25-50% and beats page-level swap on mixed hot/cold pages.

title: Ant colony's pheromone trails: route requests to replicas holding their prefix
idea: Ants follow pheromone to where the food already is. An inference router keeps a decaying radix-tree sketch (the 'pheromone') of which prompt prefixes each replica holds and sends each request to the longest match, balanced against load. Each shared prefix is then cached once per fleet instead of once per replica. A few engineer-months.
why: Fleets with long shared system prompts duplicate prefix KV on every replica. Affinity routing cuts aggregate KV memory 2-5x.

title: Mercury-lamp i-line compression chips tiled on every DIMM
idea: Move memory compression from the CPU to the memory: many slow, wide BDI/LZ compressor lanes are built in 350 nm i-line fabs (mercury arc lamps instead of neon excimer lasers, argon-free fluorine etch with N2 diluent) and tiled on the DIMM or CXL card, each lane handling a slice of bank traffic.
why: ~2x effective capacity per DIMM, with the helper silicon coming from depreciated, gas-light U.S. fabs instead of EUV/ArF lines.

title: Magnify the controller: transparent columnar transposition of records
idea: Magnify the memory controller into a layout engine: arrays of structs marked by the allocator are stored column-wise with frame-of-reference, delta and dictionary encoding, and a gather unit presents ordinary rows to the CPU.
why: Record-heavy data (logs, ORM objects, telemetry) compresses ~2-5x in columnar form without any application rewrite.

title: Epigenetic methylation bits trigger heterochromatin-style in-place page compaction
idea: Each 4 KB page carries 2 'methylation' bits set by the OS or ML runtime; methylated pages are packed by the controller into dense heterochromatin form (entropy-coded, 3-4x) inside the same DIMM while acetylated pages stay open and uncompressed. Marks are inherited by forked or copied pages, like epigenetic inheritance through cell division.
why: Capacity: software-hinted compression tier without a separate far-memory device; 30-50% fewer DRAM bits per server.

title: Swap DRAM-resident frozen weights for via-programmed 3D ROM chiplets
idea: Substitute rewritable DRAM with mask-programmed vertical ROM strings, NAND-like stacks whose bits are set by via or implant and never written, for open-weight models that stay frozen for a year. The chiplets are built on a mature U.S. line and swapped like cartridges when the model is upgraded.
why: No capacitor, no refresh and no EUV, made on domestic mature-node capital. Frees HBM for KV cache. The main risk is the model becoming obsolete, not physics.

title: Kiva-style robots shuttle memory sleds between racks on demand
idea: Borrowed from warehouse robots that bring shelves to pickers: 1-4 TB CXL memory sleds are hot-pluggable at the top of each rack, and aisle robots physically relocate sleds overnight or within minutes to racks whose forecast demand exceeds supply, steered by a cluster-wide memory demand forecaster.
why: Datacenters provision every rack for its own peak; making memory physically mobile lets the fleet buy for average demand, cutting purchased DRAM 15-30%.

title: Retired-DIMM far-memory sleds behind 180 nm bridge controllers
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: harvest DDR3/DDR4 modules from decommissioned servers into sleds run at derated speed (DDR3-800 class) by 180 nm bridge controllers with ~3 Gb/s SerDes, exposing them as a compressed far-memory tier for cold pages.
why: Millions of retired modules are shredded every year; reuse adds nearly free capacity and offsets 10-20% of new DRAM purchases with no new advanced-node silicon.

title: Procedural memory: store generator seeds instead of predictable cache lines
idea: Imposed limit: any cache line that a 16-instruction program can regenerate gets zero DRAM bytes. The memory controller detects arithmetic sequences, strided pointers, timestamp runs and repeated structs, stores a small generator descriptor in an on-die table, and synthesizes the line on read.
why: Index arrays, page tables, sparse-matrix metadata and freshly initialized buffers are highly procedural; this could save 10-30% of footprint on such workloads, beyond what zero-page detection gets.

title: Allocation leases that auto-demote unrenewed objects
idea: Worsen: let leaked and forgotten allocations live in DRAM forever. Flip: allocations carry a lease; the runtime renews leases on touch through access bits, and objects whose lease expires are migrated to a compressed far tier, with a fault bringing them back if ever touched.
why: Capacity: recovers the 10-25% of long-running service memory that is leaked or logically dead.

title: Printing-house proofreader: language-model prior corrects flipped token streams
idea: Proofreaders fix typos from context. Stored token streams (prompt histories kept in place of KV, chat logs, RAG document caches, tokenized corpora) live in 1%-BER memory with only about 3% parity. On read, a small language model does joint source-channel decoding: for each corrupted 16-bit token it scores the roughly 17 one-flip candidates by LM likelihood times channel likelihood, subject to the parity, so the redundancy in the text itself corrects the errors.
why: Text carries about 1 bit of entropy per stored character byte, so using that redundancy as the code removes most ECC overhead; combined with storing token IDs instead of KV it supports 100x memory savings for long-context serving.

title: Age-graded precision decay for the KV cache
idea: Worsen: keep every token's KV at fp16 forever. Flip: a controller-side demotion engine re-quantizes KV blocks in place as they age (fp16 to fp8 at 1k tokens, int4 at 8k, int2 at 32k, then evicts to a pooled summary vector), guided by accumulated attention mass per block.
why: Capacity: 4-6x smaller KV for long contexts with sub-1% quality loss, so more sessions per HBM stack.

title: Fiber-loop carousel broadcasts weights so no GPU stores them
idea: Worsen: give every GPU its own HBM copy of the full model. Flip: model weights circulate continuously in a WDM fiber delay loop with amplifiers; every accelerator taps the loop and runs each layer's batch as that layer's weights stream past, holding only activations locally.
why: Cost: one circulating copy serves hundreds of accelerators, so weight memory cost per accelerator drops 100x+; trades rigid layer-synchronous scheduling and optical engineering.

title: Tiny hypernetwork generates layer weights on the fly
idea: Worsen: store every weight of a large network explicitly. Flip: store a small hypernetwork plus per-layer embeddings, and generate each layer's weight tiles in SRAM just before use, never materializing the full model in DRAM.
why: Cost: 50-200x smaller model footprint; trades extra compute and some accuracy (requires training for generation).

title: Swap long agent context for sleep-phase consolidation into LoRA weights
idea: Substitute context with weights, the way the hippocampus hands memories to the cortex. A long-running agent periodically 'sleeps', distills its accumulated KV context into a small LoRA delta by test-time training, and then drops the KV.
why: A multi-day agent's KV grows to tens of GB. A 10-50 MB LoRA uses 100-1000x less memory, at the cost of extra compute and some recall error.

title: Magnify dictionaries: hardware zstd for in-memory logs and JSON
idea: Magnify compression context with trained multi-MB dictionaries per data type (logs, JSON, traces). A CXL-module decompressor at 50 GB/s serves reads, and the in-memory store keeps everything compressed.
why: Log, trace and JSON stores compress 10-20x with trained dictionaries, giving >=10x capacity on the same DIMMs.

title: Phase-interleaved co-tenancy: two jobs time-share the same physical bytes
idea: Imposed limit: every byte must be live more than 90% of the time. A scheduler pairs jobs whose memory-phase curves complement each other (prefill vs decode, forward vs backward, map vs reduce), and the compiler emits deterministic memory timetables so job B's peak lands in pages that job A has provably freed.
why: Accelerators provisioned for peak leave 30-50% of DRAM-time idle; timetabled sharing raises utilization and cuts installed DRAM 1.3-2x.

title: Goodman shadow-casting optical multiplier with laser-written weight masks
idea: Revive Goodman's 1978 incoherent optical matrix-vector multiplier: an LED/microLED row carries the input vector, light passes through a grayscale weight mask written by the university laser writer or e-beam, and a photodiode column sums each row; swapping masks swaps models.
why: Weights become a photomask instead of DRAM bits and are read by photons in parallel, so fixed edge models need no weight memory or weight bandwidth.

title: RAID-5 parity across DIMMs replaces per-rank chipkill
idea: Combine RAID-5 striping with main memory: one parity DIMM covers a group of 4-8 data DIMMs, a per-line CRC carried in burst metadata detects errors, and reconstruction from parity runs only when a CRC fails, replacing per-rank ECC devices.
why: Reliability overhead drops from 12.5-25% of bits to ~6-12% at similar device-failure tolerance.

title: Printed antifuse golden-page library for hardware dedup
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a cheap printed one-time-programmable antifuse sheet is burned at rack install with the fleet's most common read-only pages (kernel text, glibc, Python runtime, base container layers). Memory controllers map any matching page to the printed copy and keep only a small DRAM/SRAM cache of its hottest lines to hide the slow printed reads.
why: Common pages recur in every VM; a write-once printed library takes them out of DRAM (~5-15% per host) for almost no capex.

title: CDMA embedding tables: superposed rows with orthogonal spreading codes
idea: Like CDMA letting many phones share one channel, rarely accessed embedding rows of different IDs are summed into the same physical row after multiplying by pseudo-random +/-1 codes; a lookup multiplies by the ID's code to despread, leaving the others as low-level noise.
why: Recommender embedding tables are TB-scale with a long tail; 4-16x compression of tail rows with graceful noise instead of hard hash collisions.

title: Tetris player clears lines: mesh fragmented pages without moving objects
idea: A Tetris player clears half-empty rows. A meshing allocator finds two virtual pages whose live objects don't overlap in offset, copies one into the other, and remaps both virtual pages to the same physical frame, freeing a frame without changing any pointer. A fleet fragmentation profiler proves the payoff, and the work fits well under $1M.
why: Long-running C/C++ servers lose 15-30% of RSS to fragmentation. Meshing recovers 10-20% with no application code changes.

title: Multilevel organic charge-trap buffer for error-tolerant data
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): printed organic transistors with a solution-processed charge-trapping dielectric store 4-5 bits per cell as analog threshold shifts. Data tagged as tolerant (image tiles, training-set staging, sensor history) is parked here, and errors are accepted instead of corrected.
why: Holding approximate data at 4-5 bits per printed cell lowers the cost per stored value several-fold compared with digital printed bits, and keeps that bulk data out of DRAM.

title: Core-plane inhibit wire: bit-level write suppression for low-endurance tiers
idea: Core planes used an inhibit line to stop a bit from flipping; build the same into a university-fabbed ReRAM/PCM array, where each bit driver compares new and stored data and inhibits unchanged bits so a write pulses only the bits that change.
why: Typical writes flip 10-15% of bits; 5-10x fewer device writes stretch endurance-limited memories into a write-active DRAM-substitute role, shrinking DRAM.

title: Genome-assembler succinct structures with rank/select engines in controller
idea: From genome assemblers that squeeze terabyte de Bruijn graphs into succinct bitvectors: add hardware rank/select and Elias-Fano decode units to the memory controller so pointer-heavy structures (graphs, tries, inverted indexes, B-tree internals) are stored near entropy size yet traversed in one or two memory accesses per hop.
why: Pointer-rich data is often 5-20x larger than its information content; hardware rank/select makes succinct layouts fast enough for general use, cutting DRAM for indexes and graphs 3-10x.

title: Firefly anti-sync: scheduler de-phases co-located memory peaks
idea: Fireflies synchronize; we do the opposite: the cluster scheduler profiles each job's periodic memory peaks (optimizer steps, checkpoints, GC, batch spikes) and shifts their phases so peaks on a shared pool never coincide, then sizes the pool for the sum of averages. Pure scheduling, nothing fabricated.
why: Shared-pool DRAM falls 20-35% for periodic workloads.

title: SAGE-model university memory production for strategic buyers
idea: Core memory for SAGE was first built at MIT Lincoln Lab before industry took over; repeat that: federal funding lets university nanofabs build first-run specialty memory tiers (CCD weight streamers, back-end ROM, NDRO magnetics) for defense and national-lab systems under guaranteed purchase, then transfer the proven processes to U.S. mature-node fabs.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: domestic, no-EUV memory tiers that offset DRAM demand in strategic systems and de-risk new tiers before $1B+ fab commitments.

title: Near-DIMM dequantize-and-pool engine for embedding tables
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: merge the gather, dequantize and sum-pool steps of recommendation embedding lookups into a 180 nm logic chip on the module buffer; rows are stored as 4-bit codes with a per-row scale, and the chip expands and pools them locally, returning one FP16 vector per lookup bag.
why: Embedding tables are TB-scale and dominate recommender DRAM; in-place dequant makes 4-bit storage practical (~4x capacity) and cuts channel traffic 10-50x.

title: Ebbinghaus forgetting curve erodes low-order bits of aging data
idea: Tagged tensors (cached activations, retrieval embeddings, KV) lose least-significant bits on a forgetting schedule unless re-accessed, with each access acting as rehearsal that resets the clock; the controller periodically repacks eroded lines into denser formats.
why: Capacity: 2-3x density for approximation-tolerant aging data, with loss concentrated on rarely used items.

title: Alternative splicing assembles many fine-tuned models from shared exons
idea: A library of weight blocks (exons) is stored once; each task variant is a splice map selecting and ordering blocks plus tiny per-variant tweaks, the way one gene yields many proteins, so serving 100 fine-tunes needs one exon library rather than 100 copies.
why: Model-zoo serving: 10-50x less DRAM than full copies, sharing at block granularity beyond adapter methods.

title: Navigator's dead reckoning: cross-layer KV stored as deltas from fixes
idea: A navigator takes a full position fix occasionally and dead-reckons between fixes. Full KV is stored only for every 4th layer (the fix). The intermediate layers' KV is stored as low-rank deltas against the nearest fix and reconstructed inside the attention kernel.
why: In deep models, adjacent-layer KV differences are low-rank, giving 2.5-3.5x KV memory savings in long-context decode.

title: Cartoon animator's keyframes: video-model activations as keyframes plus sparse deltas
idea: Animators draw keyframes and let assistants fill the in-betweens. In video-generation and world-model serving, full per-frame KV and activations are kept only for keyframes every 8 frames. Other frames store sparse top-k token deltas against the nearest keyframe, since consecutive latents differ in only a few percent of tokens.
why: Video-model memory scales with frames x tokens. A 4-8x reduction makes minute-long generation fit on a single node.

title: GOP-style delta frames for in-memory replicas
idea: This is video-codec thinking applied to replication. Hot-standby replicas of in-memory databases, caches or VMs keep one full I-frame replica per rack. The other replicas hold only periodic P-frame write deltas against it plus a log, and rebuild a full copy only on failover, which takes seconds.
why: In-DRAM replication factor drops from 3 to about 1.2, saving 40-60% of DRAM in replicated stores in exchange for failover time.

title: IBM TrueNorth, fixed: delta-event storage of token activations
idea: TrueNorth's event-driven spiking design faded because spiking nets could not be trained to state of the art. Keep its useful trick of storing only changes: hidden states across adjacent tokens or frames are kept in SRAM as sparse thresholded deltas against the previous step, with periodic keyframes like a video codec.
why: Streaming inference (video, audio, agents) cuts activation/KV memory 3-10x where inputs change slowly.

title: Grandmother's leftovers: reuse cached document KV across different prompts
idea: Grandma turns yesterday's roast into today's soup. RAG documents are pre-encoded once into KV chunks stored on NVMe by content hash. At request time the retrieved chunks are spliced into the prompt's KV in any order, and only the ~10-15% of tokens at chunk boundaries or with high deviation are recomputed to repair cross-chunk attention. Software only, two engineers.
why: This removes duplicate KV for the same documents across thousands of requests and cuts prefill. RAG fleets see 3-5x less KV memory churn.

title: Scheduler anti-phases jobs' memory peaks, provisioning for p95 not peak
idea: Box: time-multiplex × cluster scheduler × job × forecast-triggered × small CXL burst pool. Each job's footprint curve is forecast (shuffle phases, eval passes, nightly batches) and jobs are packed so peaks interleave; rare collisions borrow from a small rack burst pool.
why: Servers are sized for peak and peak-to-mean ratios run 1.5–3×; anti-phase packing can cut installed DRAM 20–35%.

title: EIE sparse engine, fixed: fixed-rate tANS weights decoded at MACs
idea: EIE/Deep Compression's Huffman-coded sparse weights never took off because variable-length decode stalled lockstep hardware. Use block-fixed-rate tANS: each 256-weight block is coded to an exact bit budget with per-block tables, so parallel decoders at every MAC column run in lockstep straight from compressed SRAM.
why: Weights held at ~2.5-3 bits on SRAM-only chips: ~1.5-2x more model per mm^2 with no DRAM.

title: Eliminate object headers and pointers by compiling graphs into arenas
idea: A compiler pass converts pointer-linked object graphs into struct-of-arrays arenas addressed by implicit 32-bit indices, deleting per-object headers, 64-bit pointers and alignment padding.
why: Pointer-heavy heaps shrink 30-50%, and denser arrays also cut cache-line overfetch.

title: Million-lane printed scanner sheet filters cold data in place
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): the design trades area for speed: a square-meter printed sheet carries a million slow (~1 MHz) oxide-TFT comparators, each scanning its own patch of co-printed cold storage, for ~10^12 comparisons per second in aggregate. Filters and counts over cold datasets run in place, and only matches move into DRAM.
why: Analytics loads whole cold datasets into DRAM just to scan them; wide in-place scanning cuts DRAM staging 10-100x for selective queries.

title: Reversible computing, fixed: integer-exact reversible layers erase activation storage
idea: RevNets and reversible computing were abandoned because floating-point inversion drifts and reconstruction errors accumulate. Build transformer blocks from fixed-point additive couplings computed in modular integer arithmetic (y = x + f(x) mod 2^k), which are bit-exactly invertible, so backprop recomputes every activation from the output and stores none.
why: Training activation memory (often 50%+ of training memory) becomes O(1) in depth, with no storage of any kind.

title: Discounted soft-RAM VMs back 30% of memory with compressed tiers
idea: Box: oversubscribe × cloud pricing × VM × customer opt-in × compressed and remote backing. A VM class sells nominal memory at a discount where the coldest 30% is backed by compressed or remote memory under a published p99 fault-latency SLO.
why: Lets providers overcommit ~1.3× on installed hardware; pricing plus software only, so no new fluorinated fab inputs.

title: LHC-style hardware trigger decides which records deserve DRAM
idea: From the CERN trigger, which keeps about 1 event in 40,000 within microseconds: telemetry, log and clickstream records land in an SRAM ring on the NIC or memory controller, where a programmable L1 classifier (match-action tables plus a tiny model) promotes only 'interesting' records to DRAM and folds the rest into count-min and HyperLogLog summaries.
why: Observability, ad and security pipelines buffer 10-100x more data in DRAM than is ever queried; trigger-style early discard cuts ingest-tier DRAM 5-20x.

title: Memory Star: federal memory-efficiency label for cloud procurement
idea: Memory demand is working set x replication x headroom, and procurement measures none of the three. A GSA/DoD procurement standard would require vendors to report GB-hours per unit of work on standard benchmarks and give price preference to the top quartile, as ENERGY STAR did for watts.
why: Demand-side policy that pulls compression, dedup and right-sizing across the industry: 10-20% less DRAM fleet-wide over a few procurement cycles.

title: Gist tokens compress long system prompts into cached soft vectors
idea: IFR: shared instructions cost nothing per user. Closest with no materials: a trained compressor distills each long system prompt or document into 16-64 learned gist tokens, so every session caches the gist KV instead of thousands of prompt tokens.
why: System and RAG prompts are often 50-80% of per-session KV; 20-100x compression on that portion.

title: Minify training-data buffers: decode media at last moment
idea: Minify data-loader DRAM by keeping images, video and audio in their compressed codec form in host memory. They are decoded only inside the accelerator, tile by tile, right before the first layer (on-GPU JPEG/AV1 decoders).
why: Decoded RGB/PCM tensors are 10-20x larger than the codec bitstream, so data-pipeline host DRAM falls >=10x.

title: Tetris: memory-controller line compaction collapses fragmented heaps
idea: Like Tetris rows clearing once full, a controller-side engine migrates live 64 B lines out of sparsely occupied pages into dense pages during idle cycles, tracked by an SRAM-cached line-remap table so software pointers never change; fully emptied pages are handed back to the OS.
why: Allocator fragmentation strands 15-40% of heap DRAM in long-running services and Python/AI runtimes; reclaiming half of it is ~1.1-1.25x capacity.

title: Uranium enrichment cascade: concentrate hot lines into dense hot pages
idea: A centrifuge cascade separates U-235 in many small stages; the controller counts per-line accesses and, every epoch, swaps hot 64 B lines into enriched pages and cold lines into depleted pages through a line remap table, so whole depleted pages can be compressed or pushed to CXL/flash tiers.
why: Page-level tiering fails because most 4 KB pages hold a few hot lines; enrichment makes 50-70% of pages truly cold, letting local DRAM shrink ~2x with little slowdown (cost/bit).

title: TiO2 crossbars hold recommendation embedding tables with in-array gather
idea: IFR: terabyte embedding tables cost nothing. Closest with abundant elements: Ti/TiO2-x/Ti resistive crossbars (no Hf or Ta oxide) store read-mostly embedding rows rewritten monthly (endurance need ~100 cycles), and an in-array gather-sum pools the looked-up rows before anything crosses to DRAM.
why: Embedding tables dominate recommender DRAM at TB scale; displaces 80-90% of it.

title: Hibernate idle functions to flash between requests in under 1 ms
idea: Inverts 'a warm service must stay resident': after ~50 ms idle, an idle container's dirty pages are compressed and snapshotted to a CXL-attached flash tier, and the next request restores them lazily through userfaultfd prefetch of the recorded working set.
why: Serverless and microservice instances are idle >90% of the time; DRAM per hosted function drops 5-10x.

title: Million-token agents: 1-bit key sketches in DRAM, KV on flash
idea: From the extreme user of million-token AI contexts: keep a 1-bit SimHash sketch of every attention key in DRAM, use it to estimate attention scores, and fetch only the top-scoring full-precision KV blocks from CXL-attached flash through a prefetcher driven by the sketch scores.
why: Holds roughly 1/128-1/256 of the KV-cache in DRAM/HBM, turning KV capacity into a flash problem and dodging the HBM area tax (fact 6).

title: Spacecraft execute-in-place: run code straight from CXL flash
idea: From spacecraft that execute directly from radiation-tolerant NOR to spare scarce RAM: servers map binaries, shared libraries and read-only model files execute-in-place from CXL-attached flash modules with an on-module SRAM/DRAM line cache, so no page-cache copy is made in host DRAM.
why: Code and read-only data are 10-25% of server DRAM and are duplicated per container; XIP shrinks that to a small module cache.

title: Vending machine: bill memory per compressed resident byte-second
idea: Pay for what drops out of the machine: cloud providers meter memory by actual resident bytes after compression and dedup, sampled each second, instead of allocated GB, plus a discounted 'evictable' class; every developer gains a direct reward for compressing, freeing and sharing.
why: Shifts incentives fleet-wide; a 10-20% footprint cut across cloud demand equals several fabs of output during the shortage.

title: Inventory carrying cost: bill cold resident memory like warehouse stock
idea: Manufacturers price inventory by its carrying cost. Clouds and internal chargeback bill memory by touched versus untouched GB-hours (taken from page access bits): untouched pages cost 3-5x more, and pages released to a compressed tier earn a credit. Teams finally get a price signal to shed cold memory.
why: Flat per-GB pricing hides the cold-page fraction (often 30-50%); a carrying-cost price signal could cut fleet DRAM 20-30% through behavior rather than hardware.

title: Magnify entropy coding to lossless BF16 exponent compression
idea: Magnify the encoder in the DMA/memory controller to an inline lossless entropy coder for floating-point exponents. BF16/FP8 exponents carry only ~2.5-3 bits of entropy, so they are Huffman/ANS-coded per 4 KB block, and mantissas and sign pass through raw.
why: A ~1.4-1.5x lossless shrink of all weights, activations and optimizer tensors, with no accuracy cost, cuts both HBM capacity and pJ/bit moved.

title: Memory insurance: fleets sized for median, peaks covered by pooled policy
idea: Imposed limit: servers are bought with P50 memory, not P99. Tenants buy 'memory insurance' units; on a peak, a rack-level compressed far-memory reserve plus eviction of preemptible jobs pays out, priced actuarially from fleet telemetry so the operator carries the statistical risk.
why: Provisioning for peak leaves 30-40% of DRAM idle; insurance-style pooling can cut installed DRAM ~20-30%.

title: Eliminate the separate swap tier: spare GPU HBM as host swap
idea: A daemon exposes the unused HBM of under-loaded inference GPUs as a compressed swap device for the host over PCIe peer-to-peer, and evicts it instantly when the GPU needs memory back.
why: Inference fleets average 30-50% unused HBM; turning that into host memory delays CPU DRAM purchases.

title: Idle inference GPUs lend free HBM as host swap
idea: Box: harvest × installed GPU fleet × 2 MB page × idle windows × PCIe/NVLink peer access. A kernel driver exposes unused HBM on idle or lightly loaded GPUs as a fast swap device for CPU hosts and reclaims it within milliseconds when a large kernel needs it.
why: Off-peak, 30–60% of fleet HBM sits empty; borrowing already-fabricated memory replaces new DIMMs and needs no new fluorinated fab chemistry.

title: Follow-the-moon: shift memory-heavy batch to regions with idle DRAM
idea: Inverts 'memory demand is local in time': a global scheduler moves memory-bound batch work (index builds, embedding generation, training-data prep) to datacenters in their night trough, where DRAM sits idle after interactive demand falls.
why: Interactive fleets are sized for diurnal peaks and leave 30-50% of DRAM idle off-peak; time-shifting avoids buying new DRAM for batch growth.

title: Bank-level attention PIM moves KV from HBM to LPDDR
idea: An HBM bit costs ~3x the wafer area of a DDR5 bit (TSVs and yield loss), yet the KV cache only needs bandwidth for one dot product. Put q.k and softmax-weighted v accumulation units at each LPDDR bank, so the KV cache lives in commodity DRAM and only scores and results cross the bus.
why: The same KV capacity for ~1/3 of the wafer area, freeing HBM for weights; internal bank bandwidth exceeds the HBM interface.

title: Per-feature byte budgets enforced in CI at contract DRAM price
idea: Box: governance × software process × service feature × every merge × bytes-per-request metric. Each service declares resident-set and bytes-per-request budgets; CI profiles memory, blocks merges over budget, and dashboards price each MB at the current DRAM contract price.
why: Software memory bloat grows ~10–20% a year; priced budgets bend demand 10–30% when DRAM costs 4× more.

title: PGO reorders struct fields fleet-wide to delete padding
idea: Rearrange fields literally: a link-time pass uses profiles to reorder struct members by size and co-access, move cold fields into side tables and rewrite every access, applied automatically across a fleet's C, C++ and Rust builds.
why: Padding and cold fields often waste 5-15% of heap bytes; a recompile reclaims them with zero new silicon, so no neon or helium fab steps.

title: Alien who sees only entropy: entropy-sized frames in CXL expander
idea: An alien observer sees information content, not 4 KB pages. A CXL Type-3 controller measures each incoming page's compressibility inline and stores it in a 512 B, 1 KB, 2 KB or 4 KB slot. A sub-page indirection table and per-class free lists track the slots, so the host sees full nominal capacity while the media holds only the entropy.
why: Server memory typically compresses 2-3x. Transparent entropy-sized storage gives 1.8-2.5x effective capacity per DRAM chip with zero OS changes, attacking cost per bit.

title: Lanthanide contraction ordering: shrink graph gaps, then stream compressed
idea: Atoms contract steadily across the lanthanides; a reordering pass (community detection plus Gorder) renumbers graph vertices so neighbors get nearby IDs, then adjacency lists are stored as gap-coded Elias-gamma/varint streams decoded by a near-memory unit, turning random neighbor reads into sequential compressed streams.
why: Graph DRAM shrinks 4-10x, and sequential compressed streaming replaces random 64 B reads at ~5.9 pJ per useful bit with ~0.3-0.5 pJ, >10x lower energy per access (energy, density).

title: Francium rows: read-once data read destructively, never restored or refreshed
idea: Francium survives only minutes; the compiler marks tensors read exactly once and dead within milliseconds (pipeline activations, streaming buffers) and places them in francium subarrays with short 128-cell bitlines and 256 B rows, where reads isolate the cell before restore, rows are excluded from refresh, and the slot is freed on read.
why: Skipping restore, refresh and full-row activation for read-once traffic targets ~10x lower energy per access (from ~5.9 pJ per useful bit toward ~0.6), and buffers recycle in milliseconds so less DRAM is reserved for staging (energy, density).

title: Live-set-sized heaps: hardware read barriers for pauseless compaction
idea: Po: the heap is exactly as big as the live data. A load-barrier ISA extension (colored-pointer check and forwarding in hardware) on a U.S.-designed core fabbed at Intel Arizona makes concurrent compacting GC nearly free, so managed heaps run at 1.1-1.2x live set instead of 2-3x headroom.
why: Java/Go/.NET heaps are routinely provisioned 2-3x live data to keep GC cheap; hardware barriers could cut managed-heap DRAM ~40%.

title: Anti-correlated memory-peak co-scheduling across a cluster
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality: profile each job's memory-over-time curve and bin-pack jobs whose peaks are anti-correlated (phase-shifted GC cycles, batch vs interactive, prefill vs decode) onto the same host, so hosts are sized for the peak of the sum instead of the sum of peaks; memory stays 'level' instead of every host being lifted to peak.
why: Fleet DRAM is sized to peaks while average use is 40-60%; 15-30% fleet DRAM reduction.

title: Erasure-coded in-memory shards replace triple DRAM replicas
idea: Instead of keeping 2-3 full DRAM replicas of hot data in in-memory databases and caches, split each object into k data plus m parity shards across nodes (e.g. 10+4 Reed-Solomon) and rebuild over RDMA when a node fails.
why: Resilience overhead drops from 2-3x to ~1.4x of the dataset: 40-55% less DRAM for replicated in-memory tiers.

title: Dandelion seeds: erasure-coded in-memory data replaces triple replicas
idea: Dandelions scatter many small seeds rather than three big ones: in-memory caches and stores (Redis, parameter servers, checkpoint shards) replace 3x DRAM replication with Reed-Solomon 10+4 striping across nodes, rebuilding lost shards from peers over RDMA. Software only.
why: Redundancy overhead drops from 200% to 40%, freeing ~50% of DRAM in replicated memory tiers.

title: Eliminate linear KV growth with holographic superposed token memory
idea: Bind each old token's key/value pair to a random unit-phase vector and add it into a fixed-size complex matrix (holographic reduced representation); the newest N tokens stay exact and older ones are retrieved approximately by unbinding.
why: KV memory becomes O(1) in context length beyond a window: 10-100x savings for million-token contexts.

title: Ship each binary with its own memory-compression dictionary
idea: Imposed limit: each GB of DRAM must hold 4 GB of apparent data. At build time the toolchain profiles heap snapshots and trains a 64 KB dictionary per object type; the binary carries it, the OS loads it into the memory controller, and each page is compressed against its app's dictionary, tagged with a per-page dictionary ID.
why: Generic hardware memory compression reaches ~1.5-2x; dictionaries trained per app could reach 3-4x on structured heaps (JSON, protobuf, JVM objects), multiplying effective capacity.

title: Log-structured SLC NAND tier with DRAM as write absorber
idea: Combine log-structured file-system writes with a CXL memory device built from SLC 3D NAND (DUV-made) plus a small DRAM buffer: evicted dirty pages are appended sequentially into erase blocks, DRAM holds the hot set and log head, and a 28 nm controller cleans segments during idle time so random writes never hit NAND directly.
why: NAND is roughly 1/10 the cost per bit and needs no EUV; moving the cold 60-70% of memory onto it cuts DRAM per server 2-3x while respecting endurance.

title: Discarded phones repurposed as networked RAM nodes
idea: Worsen: landfill over a billion phones a year, each holding 4-12 GB of LPDDR. Flip: wipe and flash phone motherboards with a minimal RDMA-over-USB/Ethernet memory server, rack them as a remote-memory tier, and erasure-code across them for reliability.
why: Cost: near-zero marginal cost per GB from sunk-cost LPDDR, over 100x cheaper; trades latency (about 10 us), management effort and density.

title: Partial-good DRAM dies salvaged via controller remap
idea: Combine wafer-sort binning with controller-side sparing: DUV-node DRAM dies that fail spec in a few banks or subarrays (normally scrapped) are sold as reduced-capacity parts with a fuse map that the memory controller reads at boot to remap around bad regions.
why: Raises usable bits per wafer by several percent with no new tools, which matters when every non-EUV wafer counts.

title: Seed-generated tensors regenerate on read instead of being stored
idea: Replace stored pseudo-random structures (random projections, LoRA bases, hashed embedding tables, init-derived weight parts) with a PRNG seed plus a few learned coefficients; an on-chip counter-based generator (Philox-style) recreates each tile at read time.
why: Storage turns into compute: 10-100x smaller footprint for the parts of models and recommenders that can be regenerated, and no DRAM traffic for them.

title: Group-technology cells: batch requests by expert-routing fingerprint
idea: Group technology puts parts with similar routings into one manufacturing cell. A router-predictor computes each request's MoE expert fingerprint from its first layers, and the scheduler batches requests that share a fingerprint. Each GPU then stages only a small 'kit' of experts in HBM, while the rest stay in host DRAM or flash and are swapped per cell.
why: MoE models normally keep every expert resident; batching by fingerprint cuts resident expert memory 3-8x, with high reuse of each staged expert.

title: Tantalum charge wells: matrix-vector products by DRAM charge sharing
idea: Tantalum capacitors pack charge densely; weights sit in DRAM subarrays as charge, and activating several wordlines at once while bitlines are driven with input-coded pulses sums charge on each bitline in proportion to a weighted sum, read by a 4-bit ADC per column group, so GEMV happens in the array and only results leave it.
why: Only outputs cross the I/O and no row is read out bit by bit, so energy per MAC-equivalent access falls 10-30x, and low-precision analog weights need fewer cells per weight (energy, density).
